title: Your New Grip Number: Did It Actually Change? (Your finger tendons Results)
description: Your grip number from ninety days ago is on the record: towel hang, pinch hold, the works. Today the retest reads the results. Did your finger tendons actually change? Bring both old numbers, because fingers improve quietly and only the retest can prove it.

scenes.narration: Ninety days ago | you tested your grip. | Towel over the bar. | Pinch block in hand. | Two numbers went on record. | Today we measure again. | Same towel, same fold. | Same pinch setup, same weight. | Hang until a hand opens. | Pinch until it slides. | No chalk upgrades. | No thinner towel tricks. | Same hard rules as day one. | Write the new pair down | beside the old pair. | Four numbers, two dates. | At the end, | we read the results together | and decide if your fingers | truly changed, | or just had a good day.

scenes.label: HOW GRIP RESULTS ARE READ
scenes.sub: one up one flat is normal - both up is a system change
scenes.narration: Grip results are read as a pair, never as a single number, and here is why. The towel hang grades your finger flexor tendons under your full bodyweight. The pinch grades your thumb, the one grip muscle that can truly grow. If both numbers climbed, the whole grip system changed, top to bottom. If the pinch climbed and the hang stalled, your thumb out-trained your fingers, and the program needs rebalancing. If the hang climbed and the pinch stalled, your cables improved while your thumb waited its turn. Every pattern is a different prescription, which is exactly why this channel tests the pair and reads them together.

Look at what ninety days does inside a finger. The flexor tendon slides through a series of pulleys every time you grip, and hard training stresses both the cable and the pulley rings that guide it. Given months of spaced, heavy work, the tendon lays down aligned collagen and the whole sliding system gets more tolerant of friction and load. Nothing about this shows in a mirror. Your fingers will look like your fingers forever. But a towel hang reads the upgrade directly, because the towel removes every trick and leaves only tendon, pulley, and the forearm engine behind them. Quiet tissue, loud test. One more detail lives between the two tests, and it is the one coaches watch first. The order matters. This channel tests the towel hang before the pinch, because a fatigued thumb lies about the fingers, while fresh fingers tell the truth about themselves. If you ever ran the pair in the wrong order on day one, your old pinch number was graded on a tired hand and today's gap overstates the thumb's progress. Standards sound boring until they save you from a wrong conclusion. Then they sound like the whole method.

beats.title: CABLES AND PULLEYS BOTH ADAPT
lines: Months of spaced load rebuild the slide.

scenes.narration: Now the honest reading of your hang gap. Finger flexor endurance improves in a known order. First, the ring and pinky fingers stop quitting early, because they were the most undertrained. Then the whole hand lasts longer as the strong fingers share work more evenly. Grip studies see the same sequence: distribution first, duration second. So if your new hang ends with all fingers letting go together instead of the pinky peeling first, your system genuinely reorganized, even if the clock gained only a few seconds. And if the clock gained a lot while the pinky still peels first, expect the next ninety days to be slower, because the easy distribution gains are already spent. One more reading of the ending deserves emphasis, because it predicts the future. Hands that fail together improve together: the system has no single traitor left, so the next gains come from the whole chain rising at once. Hands that still fail pinky-first have a named project with a known address, and named projects are the fastest kind. Either way, today's ending wrote next season's first training note. Read it before you write anything else in the log.

beats.title: HOW IT ENDS IS DATA
lines: Together beats pinky-first, at any time.

beats.text: READ THE ENDING, NOT JUST TIME

scenes.narration: The pinch result deserves its own paragraph, because the thumb plays by different rules. The thenar muscles at the base of your thumb are real, growable muscle, fed by tendons like everything else but capable of genuine size change in ninety days. That is why pinch numbers often jump embarrassingly fast compared to hang numbers, and why this channel refuses to let a big pinch gain disguise a stalled hang. Celebrate the thumb, absolutely. Then look at what it is telling you: muscle adapts in weeks, tendon in months, and your grip contains both clocks running side by side in the same hand. Your results are those two clocks, photographed. And the two clocks in your hand explain a frustration many men misread. When the pinch soars and the hang crawls, men often conclude the hang work is broken. It is not broken; it is tendon-paced, and tendon pacing looks like failure only to men comparing it to muscle's speed. The correct comparison for the hang is last season's hang, nothing else. Clocks do not compete. They accumulate, each in its own currency, and the pair is rich when both currencies are counted honestly.

beats.text: THE THUMB RUNS A FASTER CLOCK

scenes.narration: The reframe for grip results day is the one that keeps skinny guys training. Grip is the least visual strength in the body, which makes it the easiest to abandon, because nothing in the mirror applauds it. But grip is also the strength other people actually feel: in a handshake, in a carried suitcase, in a training partner's honest surprise. Ninety days of invisible work bought you a grip that introduces itself before you say a word. The heavy guys at the gym built what photographs well. You built what functions, in the one system where your lighter frame let you practice more than any of them.
Now we train the pair together. Four rounds: twenty-five seconds of pinch hold, thirty-five to rest, and finish each round with a short towel hang. Thumb and fingers, one session, no favorites.

Your next-level protocol reads directly off your pattern. Both up: raise the difficulty, thicker towel, heavier pinch, and keep the rhythm. Pinch up and hang flat: shift two sessions a week toward towel and finger work until the pair balances. Hang up and pinch flat: add thumb work twice a week and stop letting it coast. Both flat: do not add intensity, add consistency, because flat pairs after ninety days almost always mean the sessions were too scattered for tendons to bank progress. The mistakes to retire: changing towel thickness between tests, skipping the extension work that keeps fingers healthy, and judging a pair by its better half. One weekly detail balances the whole grip program: the extensor day. Rubber band finger opens, reverse wrist work, and full open-hand stretches, once a week without exception. Grip systems that only close eventually jam their own cables, and the fingers you are building deserve a tunnel that stays open. The strongest hands in any gym are not the tightest. They are the ones that open as completely as they close.

scenes.label: THE GRIP VERDICT
scenes.sub: comment all four numbers - old pair and new pair
scenes.narration: So, did your grip actually change? If both numbers climbed, yes, completely: the whole system, cables and thumb together, is different tissue and different wiring than ninety days ago. If one climbed and one stalled, you changed exactly where you trained, which is the most coachable result there is. If both stalled, the honest verdict is not yet, and consistency, not intensity, is the missing ingredient nine times out of ten. Comment all four numbers below, the old pair and the new pair, and set the next grip retest thirty days out. Fingers change quietly. Pairs of numbers catch them at it.

Two tests, four numbers, ninety days, and your hands have a new story to tell. Keep the pair balanced, keep the towel honest, and bring me stronger fingers next retest. Subscribe so grip day never gets skipped. This is {channel}. Train the cable.
